title: Tunisia's summer electricity peak reached a record 5,089 MW by September 2026 while modelled summer 2026 margins are tight; imports and demand measures are reported, not shown to be effective

rootCauses.cause: Generation capacity additions have lagged peak-demand growth; the World Bank attributes system tightness to low investment and reports financial constraints that have exacerbated STEG's capacity expansion plan and affected distribution investment.
Thermal generation availability falls in high temperatures, when demand peaks; the World Bank says this reduced the real reserve capacity below 10% at the 2022 peak.
High temperatures and cooling consumption drive the summer maximum; STEG's communications director was also reported by Webdo saying heat damaged lines and equipment during the July 2023 peak.

Delays in projects and slow procedures and authorisations are cited by the electricity workers' union; a parliamentary committee chair separately attributes delays to a 2018 choice to abandon the Skhira thermal project in favour of solar projects. These are tier C attributed accounts, not independently documented causal findings.

dataGaps: The 5,089 MW ONEM value is a record in the January-September 2026 bulletin and is not a complete calendar-year maximum. Press/MP accounts later put an unvalidated peak near 6,000 MW. It remains unclear whether those accounts estimate unconstrained demand, use another period or method, or are inaccurate (SRC-TG-100, SRC-TG-228, SRC-TG-233).

The 770 MW peak-hour shortage risk appears in the 2025 World Bank appraisal's description of demand growth and lagging investment in 2016-2022; the PAD does not specify the exact assessment year or methodology. The 770 MW shortage-risk estimate is reported in the 2025 appraisal against the stated 2016-2022 demand-growth context; its exact assessment year and method are not identified (SRC-TG-105).

Volume, duration, affected areas and operational cause of load shedding in July 2023 and summer 2026 remain unconfirmed in STEG or regulator operational data. The July 2023 report attributes periodic shedding to STEG but cites a journalist's account; July 2026 scheduled cuts are reported by press, while another report describes STEG notices as technical-work interruptions (SRC-TG-227, SRC-TG-228, SRC-TG-233).
The World Bank PAD mentions a nationwide blackout in 2023 without date or cause; it has not been equated with the July 2023 press-reported periodic load shedding (SRC-TG-105, SRC-TG-227).

The PAD reports the 2016-2022 peak-hour shortage risk as 770 MW, about 16% of peak demand, but provides no calculation method in the cited passage. Do not treat this appraisal estimate as an observed shortage or an annual event count (SRC-TG-105).

The 2022 World Bank reserve comparison and 2026 Med-TSO seasonal model use different periods, system definitions and assumptions. Med-TSO's zero margin is a worst-case thermal margin in July-August, not an observed nationwide reserve or proof of realized unserved load; its assessment also assumes interconnection support and characterizes the executive-summary isolated risk as moderate, while a later section says high (SRC-TG-224, SRC-TG-234).

Med-TSO's P95 sensitivity narrative labels seasonal results as LOLE, while the formal methods section distinguishes P95/P50 loss-of-load duration (LOLD) from expected LOLE. Retain these figures only as source-labelled sensitivity results pending clarification (SRC-TG-234).

Peak-hour imports from Algeria and Libya during the reported 2023 and 2026 shortages were not established. The 700 MW Algeria-Tunisia exchange above the established NTC refers to summer 2025 only (SRC-TG-234).

The MP and union deficit figures for July-August 2026 range from 600 MW to 2,000 MW and lack a stated method; their estimates are politically/organizationally attributed tier C claims, not validated system measurements (SRC-TG-229, SRC-TG-230, SRC-TG-233).

The fall in STEG generation investment from TND 1.947 billion (2016-2020) to TND 248 million (2021-2025), the Skhira decision narrative, and blocked-project capacities are secondary press accounts. The primary OTE analysis and official project-decision records were not obtained (SRC-TG-228, SRC-TG-233).
STEG annual activity reports for 2023 and 2024 were not located; the accessible 2023 CMF filing contains financial statements only.

No governorate-level supply-quality series or documented water-supply/irrigation impacts from the cited 2023 or 2026 events were found. ONEM reports Jan-Sep 2026 HV/MV sales shares of 12% for water pumping/sanitation and 9% agriculture; these indicate exposure, not documented outage impacts (SRC-TG-100).

sections.heading: Problem
sections.content: Tunisia's electricity demand peaks in summer, and official annual peak records show a longer-run rise: ONEM's chart labels 3,465 MW in 2014, while its September 2026 bulletin reports a January-September record of 5,089 MW (SRC-TG-100). The peak was 4,825 MW in 2023, 4,888 MW in 2024 and 4,837 MW in 2025 (SRC-TG-220, SRC-TG-223, SRC-TG-221), so year-to-year movement is not monotonic. Capacity adequacy is tight under heat: the World Bank reports less than 10% real reserve capacity at the 2022 peak, and Med-TSO's pre-summer 2026 model shows zero worst-case thermal margin in July-August while treating 500 MW of import capacity as practically necessary (SRC-TG-224, SRC-TG-234). Med-TSO models seasonal loss-of-load risk even when interconnected, while actual 2023 and 2026 load-shedding episodes remain press-reported rather than confirmed by published operational statistics (SRC-TG-227, SRC-TG-228, SRC-TG-233, SRC-TG-234).

sections.heading: Root causes
sections.content:
Demand growth and constrained available generation coincide in hot summer periods. The World Bank states that peak demand grew by more than 4% annually over 2010-2021 and 5.5% annually over 2016-2022, while new generation investment lagged. It says the government estimated a need for 400-600 MW of additions every two years, compared with about 100 MW per year of capacity growth “in the last few years” (SRC-TG-224). The same appraisal attributes system tightness to low investment and says STEG's financial situation exacerbated implementation of its capacity-expansion plan and affected distribution investment (SRC-TG-105, SRC-TG-224).

Heat reduces thermal unit output at the same time that cooling consumption raises demand. The World Bank links the 2022 real reserve below 10% to degraded gas-unit performance in high temperatures, coincident with peak demand; Med-TSO likewise attributes the July-August maximum to high temperatures and cooling consumption (SRC-TG-224, SRC-TG-226). STEG's director of cooperation and communication was reported by Webdo in 2023 as saying heat damaged lines and equipment while demand rose; this is an attributed statement, not a documented finding (SRC-TG-227).

Project delays and the 2018 Skhira decision are possible institutional contributors, but the evidence is attributed tier C testimony. The electricity workers' union cites slow procedures, authorisations and delayed projects; an MP attributes project delays to abandoning Skhira in favour of solar development (SRC-TG-229, SRC-TG-233). The reported 87% fall in STEG generation investment and blocked or delayed project capacities relay an OTE analysis through press, whose primary report was not opened (SRC-TG-228). These accounts do not independently establish how much each factor contributed to the measured adequacy risk.

Imports and demand measures are reported for tight periods, but the sources do not show that they were effective. The World Bank's 2023 appraisal says electricity imports met 12% of demand in 2023 (SRC-TG-105). Med-TSO reports the Algeria-Tunisia exchange reached 700 MW, above the established transfer capacity, to cover a significant adequacy shortfall in summer 2025 (SRC-TG-234). Its 2026 outlook describes commercial-lighting and air-conditioning restrictions, off-peak tariff incentives, voluntary industrial curtailment and discussions with Algeria on temporary import increases; these are measures and negotiations reported before the summer, not evidence that each was implemented or that load was served in a specific later event (SRC-TG-234).

sections.heading: Evidence
sections.content:
- **Observed annual peak demand:** ONEM's monthly series labels 3,465 MW in 2014, 4,025 MW in 2017, 4,247 MW in 2019, 4,472 MW in 2021, 4,677 MW in 2022, 4,825 MW in 2023 and 4,888 MW in 2024. The same September 2026 chart shows 5,089 MW in 2026; its text explicitly says this is the record “à fin septembre” (through September), not a final calendar-year total. ONEM reports 4,837 MW for full-year 2025 (SRC-TG-100, SRC-TG-220, SRC-TG-221, SRC-TG-223). The rise from 2014 to the 2026 through-September record is about 47%, a calculation from the two ONEM values, not a separately published statistic (SRC-TG-100).
- **Historical capacity and reserve context:** The World Bank reports 6,015 MW installed capacity and a 4,678 MW peak in 2022, calling the reserve margin 22%; it states real reserve capacity was less than 10% due to heat-related gas-unit derating. The 22% is the surplus as a share of installed capacity; calculated as a share of peak demand, the nominal surplus is about 28.6%. The World Bank's separate 770 MW peak-hour shortage-risk estimate is reported in the 2025 appraisal in the context of 2016-2022 demand growth and lagging investment, but its exact model base year is not given (SRC-TG-105, SRC-TG-224).
- **Seasonal model, not observed outcome:** Med-TSO's Summer Outlook 2026 gives seasonal LOLE of 81 hours isolated and 39 hours interconnected under normal conditions, with EENS of 27,786 and 12,572 MWh respectively. For its P95 sensitivity it reports 219 and 122 hours and 82,028 and 37,423 MWh; its methods terminology for these P95 durations is inconsistent, as noted in `data_gaps`. The model's weekly peak reaches 5,827 MW across 36 climatic years; average available thermal capacity is about 5,000 MW, with a minimum average daily available value of 3,100 MW. Its worst-case hourly thermal margin reaches zero from late June through July and August. These are modeled seasonal adequacy results, published before the summer, not measurements of actual outages or unserved energy (SRC-TG-234).
- **Imports and annual import dependence:** ONEM's 2023 bulletin reports 2,496 GWh of purchases from Algeria and Libya and 21,809 GWh “available for local market” (11% of local-market needs in ONEM's text); the World Bank separately says imports covered 12% of electricity demand in 2023. Their scopes/denominators may differ, so the two should not be forced to agree. Med-TSO's 700 MW above-NTC flow concerns summer 2025, not 2026 (SRC-TG-220, SRC-TG-105, SRC-TG-234).
- **Reliability indicators:** The World Bank TEREG appraisal reports 2023 SAIDI of 137 minutes and a programme target of 128 minutes by 2028. It separately says storms drove energy not supplied (ENS) from 6.3 GWh in 2018 to 10 GWh in 2019. Its 2023 “nationwide blackout” reference has no date or cause in the cited passage (SRC-TG-105).
- **Press-reported events and estimates:** Webdo reported periodic load shedding in some regions on 20 July 2023, alongside the official peak of 4,825 MW; the article's statement that STEG adopted shedding is journalistic attribution. In 2026, Webmanagercenter reported scheduled cuts in July and a peak near 6,000 MW based on unnamed sources and MPs; Webdo reported an MP's 1,500 MW deficit claim on 28 July; La Presse reported an MP's 600 MW claim on 25 July and the union's 2,000 MW estimate on 25 August. The peak and deficit estimates are unverified tier C claims and conflict with the official 5,089 MW record through September (SRC-TG-227, SRC-TG-228, SRC-TG-229, SRC-TG-230, SRC-TG-233, SRC-TG-100).

sections.heading: Why confidence is what it is
sections.content: Confidence is medium for a current adequacy concern: the observed ONEM peak series is a tier A official source, and the 2022 reserve figures and separate 2026 seasonal model come from tier B institutional sources. They establish rising historical peaks and modeled heat-season tightness, but do not provide one directly comparable observed firm-capacity time series through 2026. The 2026 summer model is a projection/scenario, not an observed outage record. Load-shedding claims and disputed 2026 deficits are tier C reports; the causes assigned to permitting delays, Skhira and the investment collapse are also not independently confirmed. The draft therefore retains those claims only with attribution and explicit gaps.

sections.heading: Links to other sectors
sections.content:
- **Water:** ONEM reports water pumping and sanitation as 12% of high- and medium-voltage sales in January-September 2026 (SRC-TG-100). This indicates potential exposure to electricity interruptions; no documented water-supply impact from the cited episodes was found.
- **Agriculture:** Agricultural pumping accounted for 9% of high- and medium-voltage sales in January-September 2026, and its sales grew 5% year on year (SRC-TG-100). No sourced irrigation impact from the cited outages was found.

sections.heading: Leads for phase 2
sections.content:
- TEREG programme (World Bank, P507304), including SAIDI and loss-reduction indicators and a 10-year least-cost investment plan: https://documents1.worldbank.org/curated/en/099041025150537909/text/BOSIB-5b68fe2f-7a73-435b-930b-ec670325463c.txt
- ELMED Tunisia-Italy interconnector (World Bank, P179240): https://projects.worldbank.org/en/projects-operations/project-detail/P179240
- Skhira power plant and Kairouan solar project (claims and status require primary project records; SRC-TG-228, SRC-TG-233).
- Summer demand-reduction measures, off-peak tariffs and voluntary industrial curtailment described in Med-TSO's outlook (SRC-TG-234).

sections.heading: Verification
sections.content:
Dated national peaks and the published adequacy studies have different periods and methods. The official peak series is used for observed values. Press accounts are attributed as reports; undocumented comparisons and residual capacity estimates do not establish actual outages.

**Independent review, 21 November 2026:** pass after corrections. Checked ONEM Conjoncture énergétique, September 2026 (SRC-TG-100, demand paragraph: 5,089 MW to end-September 2026 against 4,837 MW at end-September 2025); Med-TSO Summer Outlook 2026 (SRC-TG-234, normal-conditions results 81 h and 39 h, P95 219 h and 122 h, Tunisia measures paragraph, 700 MW Algeria-Tunisia exchange); World Bank ELMED PAD (SRC-TG-224, page 8, reserve paragraph: 22% nominal margin, real reserve less than 10%); Webdo 20 July 2023 (SRC-TG-227), Webdo 28 July 2026 (SRC-TG-233), La Presse 25 July 2026 (SRC-TG-230) and 25 August 2026 (SRC-TG-229). Corrections: title no longer says the peak "is rising" or that imports and demand response "support adequacy"; it now states the dated record and that measures are reported, not shown to be effective. The July 2023 heat-damage statement is attributed to STEG's communications director as reported by Webdo. The MP's surname is given as Kettari with the Ktari variant noted. The 2023 import purchases and available-for-market values are corrected to the ONEM December 2023 bulletin values (2,496 GWh and 21,809 GWh; SRC-TG-220). The reviewer's objection to the "below 10%" reserve wording was not confirmed: the full World Bank sentence reads "less than 10 percent" and links it to degraded gas-unit performance at high temperature. The Med-TSO outlook text on measures for Tunisia (lighting and air-conditioning restrictions, off-peak tariffs, voluntary industrial curtailment, talks with Algeria) was read; it describes measures, not their effect. Independent teammate sign-off is outstanding; reviewer and author share the TahaGHZ identity, so the record is not validated.

capacity grew only about 100 MW a year. In 2022 installed capacity was 6,015 MW against a
4,678 MW peak, a nominal 22% reserve margin. The real reserve was under 10% because gas units
lose output in high temperatures, which is when the peak occurs.

Page 12, para. 17:

> [...] the interconnector would integrate the embryonic Maghreb electricity market with that of Europe, thus increasing electricity exchanges between Tunisia and Algeria (currently about 122 GWh per year), and possibly Libya once the interconnector between Tunisia and Libya can be made to operate properly.

English gloss: exchanges with Algeria were about 122 GWh a year. The Tunisia-Libya
interconnector did not operate properly at the time of writing.

Page 13, para. 19 (history):

> On this basis, a joint Tunisian-Italian group met in September 2005 and approved a project option consisting of a 1,000 MW submarine cable and a 1,200 MW power plant in Tunisia, of which 800 MW was for export to Italy. [...] In 2011, the situation changed with the recession in Europe—resulting in a surplus of electricity on the Italian side—and the economic slowdown since 2011 in Tunisia. The two sides agreed to revise the interconnector project concept, which led to the elimination of the proposed power plant in Tunisia, the reduction of the cable's capacity (to 600 MW), and the change in the expected direction of power flows in the short term (that is, from Italy to Tunisia).

English gloss: the 2005 concept was a 1,000 MW cable and a 1,200 MW export power plant in
Tunisia. After 2011 the plant was dropped, the cable was cut to 600 MW, and the expected
short-term flow was reversed to run from Italy to Tunisia.

Page 13, para. 20:

> The Elmed interconnector has an estimated total cost of €964.2 million covering investments on the Tunisian and Italian sides. [...] (a) Sicily-Tunisia 200 km submarine cable and two HVDC converter stations in Tunisia and Sicily (estimated cost: €840 million), (b) Tunisian grid reinforcement (estimated cost: €110 million) [...]

English gloss: total cost about €964.2 million, of which €840 million is for the 200 km cable and
the two converter stations and €110 million for reinforcing the Tunisian grid.

Page 31, para. 66:

> Among other things, the Elmed interconnector contributes to improving the reliability of the Tunisian power system (thus reducing load shedding) [...] In the base case, while Tunisia will be a net electricity importer in 2030 (net imports of 663 GWh in 2030), the situation is reversed in 2040 when the country starts exporting an important amount of RE to both Italy and Algeria [...] During the summer season and in particular during evening peaks, as the country's thermal capacity is more expensive or insufficient to cover the peak load, Tunisia mostly relies on imports from Italy and (to a lower extent) on Algeria to ensure system reliability. [...] In the reduced RE development scenario, Tunisia is a net electricity importer from Italy in both 2030 and 2040, with imports highest in summer months.

English gloss: the model expects ELMED to reduce load shedding. In the base case Tunisia is a net
importer in 2030 (663 GWh) and a net exporter of renewable power by 2040. On summer evening peaks,
when Tunisian thermal capacity is too costly or insufficient, Tunisia relies mainly on imports
from Italy. With slower renewable growth, Tunisia stays a net importer from Italy in 2030 and
2040.

Page 34, para. 72:

> Although it has been able to guarantee reliable electricity supply, STEG's commercial performance has been declining due to increasing losses and nonpayment, which has become more pronounced since the revolution (total losses increasing from 12 percent in 2010 to 21 percent in 2021; while payment among private customers is more than 95 percent, nonpayment is 50 percent from public customers, resulting in accumulated arrears of around 20 percent of total turnover).

English gloss: total losses rose from 12% (2010) to 21% (2021), more markedly since 2011. Private
customers pay more than 95% of bills; public customers leave 50% unpaid.

Page 48, results framework:

> Reduction in System Average Interruption Duration Index (SAIDI) (Percentage) 0.00 50.00

English gloss: the project targets a 50% cut in SAIDI. No baseline value in minutes is given.
resolvedSources.notes:
Page numbers are the "Page n of 68" footers in the World Bank text version. The planning
assumptions (400-600 MW every two years) are attributed to the Government of Tunisia without a
document reference. The flow projections come from the World Bank's VRE Integration study
(dispatch model), which is not public.

> In 2027, forecasted monthly consumption ranges from 1,668 GWh to 2,699 GWh, while monthly peak demand varies from 3.4 GW to 6.8 GW. Because of this monthly load distribution, maintenance of thermal power plants is not allowed during summer (June–August).

English gloss: the peak used is the highest hourly value across 36 simulated climate years, so

2030, up 0.9 GW (13.2%). The maximum comes in July-August because of heat and cooling demand.

English gloss: assumed installed capacity is 7,316 MW (2027) and 10,520 MW (2030). Assumed import

> In 2027, the results show frequent periods where the margin approaches zero, particularly during July and August, but also scattered across other months. This indicates a tight adequacy situation, with limited reserve available to cover unexpected outages or demand spikes.

However, critical hours with minimal margin persist, requiring careful operational planning and the potential support of imports or storage to ensure system reliability.

English gloss: in 2027 the thermal margin often nears zero, especially in July-August. By 2030
risk is lower if capacity grows as assumed, but critical hours remain.

> In 2027, adequacy concerns emerge mainly during July and August, coinciding with high demand and lower TPP availability. Printed p. 17:

> For the 2030 horizon as seen in Figure 10, we considered that Tunisia and Italy plan to commission their first electricity interconnection project by year 2028.

> The 500 kV power line will run from the electrical substation at Partanna (Sicily) to the substation at Mlaabi on the Tunisian peninsula of Capo Bon, for a total length of 220 km (200 km of which is undersea cable). It will have a capacity of 600 MW and a maximum depth of approximately 800 m, along the Strait of Sicily.

English gloss: the 2030 case assumes ELMED is commissioned by 2028. It is a 600 MW, 500 kV link
from Partanna (Sicily) to Mlaabi (Cap Bon), 220 km long, of which 200 km is undersea.

Printed p. 10, footnote 1:

> Data for Algeria & Libya are missing from this assessment due to limited engagement from their side.

> TN | 24 | 27 | 13% | 4.10%

English gloss: Tunisia's average annual consumption is 24 TWh in 2027 and 27 TWh in 2030, +13%,

Printed p. 11:

> In Egypt, Morocco, and Tunisia, the summer peak demand (26 May to October 2nd) aligns closely with the maximum demand due to increased air conditioning loads during high-temperature periods.

English gloss: in Tunisia the annual maximum falls in summer because of air-conditioning load.

Printed p. 24, section 4.2, Table 11 (2027) and Table 12 (2030), "Exchanges needed to overcome adequacy risks", Tunisia rows (checked on page image):

> 2027: DZ00–TN00 | 2 GWh | NTC 250 / 250 MW ; LY00–TN00 | 2 GWh | NTC 250 / 250 MW
> 2030: DZ00–TN00 | 0 | 250 / 250 ; LY00–TN00 | 0 | 250 / 250 ; IT00–TN00 | 0 | 600 / 600

> Furthermore, Algeria and Libya support Tunisia to overcome adequacy risks [...]

> For the 2030 horizon (Table 12), the adequacy situation shows some significant changes compared to 2027. The exchanges required to overcome adequacy risks decrease for most North African links, with Tunisia able to rely more on internal resources.

> The Italy–Tunisia (IT–TN) interconnection, with 0GWh needed for adequacy and a bilateral NTC of 600 [M]W, indicates that Tunisia can rely on imports from Italy if necessary.

> The generation mix is dominated by gas (69%), followed by solar (25%), with smaller shares from wind (4%) and battery storage (2%). Renewable energy sources (RES) account for 30.1% of NGIC, mainly driven by solar development.

> The generation structure becomes more diversified, with gas (50%) and solar (30%) as the leading contributors, followed by wind (15%) and battery storage (5%). The 2030 capacity assumes a large build-out (NGIC 10,520 MW, RES 46.9% of capacity), which goes

of Tables 4 and 5 is misaligned and is not quoted. The 2030 LOLE figures are internally

Article body (published 2023-07-20):

> En ces derniers jours de canicule, la Tunisie a enregistré, ce jeudi 20 juillet 2023, un 3ème pic record de consommation d'électricité. peak. STEG applied periodic load shedding in some regions to relieve the network and avoid large

> Selon le directeur de la coopération et de la communication à la STEG, Mounir Ghabri, dans une déclaration à l'agence TAP, que la demande a atteint 4825 mégawatts à 12h48, dépassant la demande enregistrée en 2022 (8 septembre 2022), qui a été estimée à 4677 mégawatts.

above the 2022 record of 4,677 MW (8 September 2022).

resolvedSources.title: Crise électrique en Tunisie, l'été 2026 révèle la fracture structurelle entre demande record et sous-investissement
resolvedSources.extracts:
Article body (published 2026-08-03):

> Durant le mois de juillet 2026, la Société tunisienne de l'électricité et du gaz (STEG) a dû appliquer des coupures de courant programmées pour empêcher l'effondrement total de la boucle électrique nationale. [...] Selon des sources concordantes et des déclarations parlementaires, la pointe de consommation aurait côtoyé, voire dépassé, le niveau inédit des 6 000 mégawatts (MW), un chiffre qui attend toujours une validation technique officielle par l'opérateur public.

English gloss: in July 2026 STEG applied scheduled power cuts to prevent the national grid from
collapsing. According to unnamed sources and statements by MPs, peak consumption came close to or
exceeded 6,000 MW. The operator had not officially validated this figure.

> D'après les analyses relayées par l'Observatoire tunisien de l'économie (OTE), cette crise est l'aboutissement prévisible d'un désengagement financier massif. L'organisme estime que les investissements de la STEG dans les moyens de production se sont effondrés d'environ 87 % entre la période 2016-2020 (1,947 milliard de dinars) et 2021-2025 (248 millions de dinars). Ce sous-investissement direct a bloqué ou retardé des projets majeurs : la centrale à cycle combiné de Skhira (d'une capacité de 480 MW) ainsi que 380 MW de projets éoliens et solaires en régie directe.

English gloss: according to the OTE (a Tunisian economic watchdog), STEG's investment in
generation fell by about 87%, from TND 1.947 billion (2016-2020) to TND 248 million (2021-2025).
This blocked or delayed the 480 MW Skhira combined-cycle plant and 380 MW of STEG-owned wind and
solar projects.

> Si l'envolée des températures et l'usage intensif de la climatisation expliquent l'explosion immédiate de la demande, cette justification conjoncturelle dissimule mal une fragilité structurelle devenue critique.

English gloss: heat and heavy air-conditioning use explain the immediate jump in demand, but the
article argues the weakness is structural.

Press analysis. The ~6,000 MW peak is explicitly unconfirmed, and ONEM's official record to the

was not opened.

Page numbers are the printed footers, which match the PDF page index. Text was extracted with

p. 9, executive summary (isolated mode):

> Tunisia (TN) exhibits moderate adequacy risk, with periodic but manageable supply constraints that suggest capacity margins are tight yet not critically deficient.

p. 11, "What's new", country box:

> Tunisia facing one of its most constrained summers in recent years, Tunisia has introduced rolling demand reduction measures including restrictions on commercial lighting and air conditioning, extended off-peak tariff incentives to shift consumption away from peak hours, and appeals to industrial consumers to voluntarily curtail during critical periods. > Under normal conditions, Tunisia faces a high adequacy risk in isolated mode, with LOLE lasting approximately 81 hours and EENS reaching 27,786 MWh. [...] In interconnected mode, both dimensions of risk are reduced -- LOLE falls to approximately 39 hours and EENS to 12,572 MWh [...]

p. 26, section 4.2:

> A notable example of how countries respond to acute adequacy pressures occurred last summer on the Tunisia-Algeria (TN-DZ) corridor, where the exchange was increased to 700 MW, well above the established NTC, to address a significant adequacy shortfall in Tunisia. demand, but the N-1 security criterion was not respected on that link during that period.

p. 45, section 5.6 Tunisia, Demand:

> Tunisian seasonal weekly demand, depicted in Figure 33, ranges between 436 GWh and 619 GWh, while peak hourly demand ranges from 4,000 MW to 5,827 MW each week. It should be noted that weekly demand refers to the average values of all 36 analysed climatic years, while peak hourly demand values refer to the weekly maximum for all 36 analysed climatic years.

English gloss: the weekly peak (maximum over 36 climate years) ranges up to 5,827 MW in summer
2026.

p. 45-46:

> What makes Tunisia's situation particularly notable is the very narrow gap between total installed capacity and peak demand. Even before accounting for forced outages or maintenance, the system has minimal headroom -- making the 500 MW import capacity from neighbouring countries not a comfort measure but a practical necessity for day-to-day system balance.
